Chapter 3: The Four Common Responses to Emotional Overload
When emotions start to boil over, it’s so easy to slip into old habits—those go-to ways of coping that might feel safe in the moment, even if they don’t actually help us in the long run. Most of us don’t even realize we’re doing it. These patterns are shaped over time—by our families, the culture around us, and all the little and big experiences we’ve had. But recognizing them is the first step to choosing something better.
Picture this: one woman comes home after a rough day, feeling let down by just about everything. The smallest misunderstanding with her spouse turns into a full-blown argument. She yells, maybe slams a door. In that moment, it feels justified—like a release. But what’s left afterward? Regret. Distance. That sense that something important has been lost.
Or think of someone else, sitting through a tough meeting at work. Criticism stings, but instead of speaking up, he just smiles and nods, tucking the hurt deep inside. Later, those unspoken feelings turn into resentment, quietly shaping how he sees his coworkers and himself.
Let’s break down these common responses. First up, exploding. This is the one everyone recognizes—the raised voices, the harsh words, the urge to make yourself heard no matter what. It can feel powerful in the moment, like you’re finally letting it all out. But the reality? The aftermath is rarely what we hope for. Relationships get bruised, trust takes a hit, and the real issues just get buried deeper.
Then there’s stuffing. It’s quieter, but just as tough on us. Stuffing means swallowing your feelings, telling yourself, “It’s not a big deal,” or “I really shouldn’t feel this way.” On the outside, everything looks fine—maybe even calm. But inside, that pressure just keeps building. And over time, stuffed emotions can show up as bitterness, anxiety, or even in your body as aches and pains.
Sometimes, exploding comes with a twist—blaming someone else for your reaction. You might hear, “If you hadn’t done that, I wouldn’t have lost my temper.” This shifts the responsibility away, making it tough to learn or change. And on the flip side, some people stuff their feelings, then put on a happy face, acting like nothing’s wrong. This “stuffing and smiling” can leave you feeling lonely, even when surrounded by people you love.
Here’s something important: most of us don’t choose these responses on purpose. They’re habits—automatic, learned from years of watching and experiencing. But just because they’re familiar doesn’t mean we’re stuck with them. With awareness and a little intention, new ways of responding are absolutely possible.
One eye-opening truth? Emotions themselves aren’t bad or wrong. It’s what we do next that really counts. When you spot your go-to response, you can break the cycle—maybe by taking a deep breath, stepping away for a moment, or even reaching out to someone you trust. Sometimes, just saying, “I’m having a hard time right now,” can make all the difference.
And let’s not forget, faith has a powerful role here. There’s real comfort in knowing that change isn’t just about white-knuckling your way through. With help from something bigger than ourselves, real transformation can happen. Grace becomes a lifeline—not just for forgiving others, but for forgiving yourself when those old patterns sneak back in.
Over time, you’ll notice the grip of these responses loosening. Maybe you explode less. Maybe stuffing your feelings isn’t your first instinct anymore. Relationships start to feel safer, more honest. And instead of blame or pretending, there’s room for vulnerability and real connection. The journey isn’t about being perfect—it’s about progress, one small choice at a time.
